title.en: Yorimasa Slays the Night Monster

region.en: The Imperial palace, Kyoto

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: A shape-shifting night-haunt on the palace roof is driving the Emperor to death; the archer Yorimasa waits through thunder and lightning, brings the beast down with a single steel-headed arrow, and is rewarded with the sword King of Lions and the hand of Lady Ayame.
summary.zh: 夜怪每夜伏於紫宸殿頂，致天皇病篤；武士賴政於雷雨中張弓一箭射落此猿首虎身蛇尾之怪，獲賜獅子王之劍並娶女官菖蒲。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Japanese warrior legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An Emperor lay seriously ill, kept from sleep every night by a horrible unaccountable noise on the roof of the Purple Hall of the North Star. At sunset a dark cloud crept from the eastern horizon and settled on the palace roof, and the courtiers who waited in the imperial bedchamber heard scratching sounds as if the cloud had changed into a beast with gigantic claws. Night after night the visitant returned and the Emperor grew worse, until it was clear that unless the monster was destroyed his Majesty would die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yorimasa' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The court named Yorimasa as the one knight valiant enough for the task. He made his preparations - best bow, steel-headed arrows, armour under a hunting-dress and a ceremonial cap - and lay in concealment at sunset while thunder crashed and wind shrieked like a pack of wild demons. At midnight a black cloud rushed through the sky and stopped at the north-east corner of the roof; lightning flashed, and Yorimasa saw the gleaming eyes of a large animal. Noting the position, he bent his bow round as the full moon and shot. There was a roar of anger and a heavy thud as the monster rolled from the roof to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yorimasa' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yorimasa and his retainer ran forward and despatched the creature, which was as large as a horse, with an ape's head, the body and claws of a tiger, a serpent's tail, bird's wings, and the scales of a dragon. From the moment it died the Emperor's health improved. His Majesty ordered the skin kept for ever in the Imperial treasure-house, presented Yorimasa with the sword Shishi-wo, the King of Lions, promoted him at court, and finally gave him the Lady Ayame, most beautiful of the ladies-in-waiting.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yorimasa' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Yoshitsune and Benkei on Gojo Bridge
title.zh: 義經與弁慶五條橋之會

region.en: Gojo Bridge, Kyoto

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Trained by the King of the Tengu, the exiled boy Yoshitsune defeats the giant priest Benkei - who has collected 999 swords waylaying knights on Gojo Bridge - and wins him as a retainer for life.
summary.zh: 牛若丸（義經）受天狗之王傳授武藝，於五條大橋擊敗奪得九百九十九柄刀的強梁僧兵弁慶，弁慶遂終身追隨。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Japanese heroic legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Yoshitomo had been killed fighting the all-powerful Taira, whose cruel leader Kiyomori sought to destroy his children. Their mother Tokiwa fled into hiding and at last consented to become the hated Kiyomori's wife - the only way to save her sons' lives - keeping Yoshitsune with her and whispering daily: remember your father Minamoto Yoshitomo; grow strong and avenge his death. At seven the boy was sent to a monastery to be made a monk, but in a lonely valley he flourished a little wooden sword against the rocks, singing fragments of war-songs and longing to right the wrongs the Taira had heaped on his family.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yoshitsune and the Taira' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: One night a thunderstorm broke over the valley and a mighty giant with a long red nose, glaring eyes, bird-like claws and feathered wings stood before the boy - the King of the Tengu, ruler of the elves of the mountains. Admiring the boy's perseverance, he offered to teach him all there was to know of swordsmanship, and soon Yoshitsune could vanquish twenty small tengu at once. At fifteen he heard of Benkei, a wild giant of a bonze who waylaid knights on the Gojo Bridge of Kyoto and had already won nine hundred and ninety-nine swords. Yoshitsune went to meet him, playing his flute to show his unconcern.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yoshitsune and the Tengu' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Benkei disdained to fight what looked like a dreamy flute-playing boy, and this contempt so angered Yoshitsune that he kicked the halberd from the giant's hands. Leaping from side to side with tengu-trained agility, he mocked Benkei's swinging strokes until the giant grew weary, tripped him, and mounted triumphantly on his back. Amazed at defeat by so slight a victor - the son of Lord Yoshitomo - Benkei begged to become his retainer, and from that hour the two names were linked: together they drove the Taira to their last ruin at Dan-no-ura.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yoshitsune and Benkei Fight' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Ghost Armies of Dan-no-ura

region.en: Dan-no-ura strait, Shimonoseki

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Sailing past Dan-no-ura, Yoshitsune and Benkei meet a ghostly company of the drowned Taira clan; Benkei stills the phantoms with a rosary and prayers, and the crabs with warrior markings on their backs are said to be the ghosts of the defeated.
summary.zh: 義經與弁慶舟過壇之浦，遭平家亡靈阻擋；弁慶持數珠誦經鎮靜亡魂。漁人至今見幽軍出沒，謂背有甲紋之蟹乃平家武士之靈。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Japanese ghost legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Yoshitsune and his henchman Benkei had arranged to cross in a ship from the province of Settsu to Saikoku. When they reached Dan-no-ura a great storm arose: mysterious noises came from the towering waves, a far-away echo of the din of battle, the rushing of ships, the whirling of arrows, the footfall of a thousand men. From the lashing crests there arose a ghostly company of the Taira clan, their armour torn and blood-stained, thrusting out vaporous arms to stop the boat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Yoshitsune and Benkei Fight' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yoshitsune cried out for revenge even upon the ghosts of the Taira dead; but Benkei, always shrewd and circumspect, bade his master lay aside the sword, took out a rosary, and recited Buddhist prayers. Peace came to the great company of ghosts; the wailing ceased and the sea grew calm. Fishermen still see ghostly armies come out of the sea, wailing and shaking their long arms, and say the crabs with markings on their backs are the wraiths of the Taira warriors who drowned there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Raiko Slays the Goblin of Oyeyama

region.en: Mount Oye (Oeyama), near Kyoto

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: The Goblin King Shutendoji kidnaps and devours the young of Kyoto from his iron palace on Mount Oye; Raiko and five knight-companions go disguised as mountain priests, trick the goblins into drinking heaven-sent poison sake, and behead the monster in his sleep.
summary.zh: 大江山之鬼王酒吞童子擄食京都少年男女。賴光與四天王偽裝山伏潛入鐵宮，以神賜之毒酒灌醉群鬼，斬鬼王首級，救出被擄女子。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Japanese demon-slaying legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In the reign of the Emperor Ichijo a demon dwelt on Mount Oye who could assume many forms. Slipping into Kyoto as a human being, he left home after home destitute of well-loved sons and daughters, whom he carried back to his mountain stronghold to mock and finally devour. Even the sacred Court was not exempt: the Goblin King Shutendoji snatched away the beautiful daughter of Kimitaka, and the Emperor summoned his council to plan the creature's destruction. All agreed that the doughty knight Raiko should be sent, with chosen companions, on this perilous adventure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'The Goblin of Oyeyama' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Raiko chose five companions and bade them go disguised as mountain priests, armour hidden in unsuspicious knapsacks. Two knights prayed at the temple of Hachiman, God of War, two at the shrine of Kwannon the Goddess of Mercy, and two at the temple of Gongen. On Mount Oye's formidable path of rocks, forests, and bottomless chasms, three old men suddenly appeared - the deities themselves, now vindicating the prayers - and gave Raiko a jar of magical sake called Shimben-Kidoku-Shu, a cordial for men but poison for goblins, before vanishing into the clouds in miraculous light.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'The Goblin of Oyeyama' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: A weeping princess washing a blood-stained garment in a stream led the band to a great palace of black iron and satisfied the sentinels with the mountain-priest story. In the mighty hall sat the Goblin King, gigantic, red-skinned, with a mass of white hair, feasting on food served by captive Kyoto women. When the feast was in full swing Raiko politely offered the magic sake; the Goblin King drank one cup, then a second, and all his goblins drank until they slept. The three deities appeared once more to say the demon's limbs were bound. Raiko's sword crashed down on the monster's neck; the severed head shot into the air, pouring smoke and fire from its nostrils, and a second blow laid it dead. The knights carried out the grim head, followed by a company of happy maidens released at last.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Raiko Slays the Goblin' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Raiko and the Mountain Spider

region.en: Rendai plain and Kagura-ga-Oka, near Kyoto

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: In Kenko Hoshi's darker version, Raiko and Tsuna follow a flying skull to a ruined mansion crowded with goblins; a beautiful woman turns out to be the Mountain Spider, whose carcass bursts open to yield 1,990 human skulls.
summary.zh: 另一傳本：賴光與碓井隨飛空骷髏至廢屋，遇百鬼夜行與妖女；妖女實為山蜘蛛，斬其腹竟湧出一千九百九十顆骷髏。

sensitivity.note: Medieval yokai legend (Kenko Hoshi variant) recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In another version, written by Kenko Hoshi, Raiko left Kyoto with Tsuna, the most worthy of his retainers, and as they crossed the plain of Rendai a skull rose in the air and flew before them like a wind-driven thing until it vanished at Kagura-ga-Oka. There they found a ruined mansion where an old woman of strange aspect, dressed in white with white hair, opened her eyes with a small stick and let her breasts fall upon her knees. 'I am two hundred and ninety years old,' she said; 'I serve nine masters, and the house in which you stand is haunted by demons.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Another Version' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the kitchen Raiko saw a storm brewing, heard ghostly footsteps, and watched a great company of goblins crowd into the room. Then came a nun-like being with a face two feet long and arms white as snow and thin as threads, which laughed and vanished like mist; and when a cock crowed, a lovely woman appeared instead, more graceful than willow branches waving in the breeze. Her radiant beauty blinded him for a moment, and he found himself enveloped in countless cobwebs; he struck with his sword, and she disappeared, leaving the blade buried in the floor planks, its point broken, and covered with white blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Another Version' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Search uncovered a den where a monster lay with many legs and an enormous downy head, its mighty eyes shining like sun and moon as it groaned that it was sick and in pain. The broken sword-point projected from its body; Raiko and Tsuna dragged it out and cut off its head, and from the wound in its stomach gushed nineteen hundred and ninety skulls, with spiders as large as children. Within the entrails were the ghostly remains of human corpses: the monster was the Mountain Spider.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'Another Version' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Momotaro, or the Son of a Peach

region.en: A mountain village and the Demon Island of the North-Eastern Sea (symbolic pin)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: An old couple find a boy born from a peach; at fifteen Momotaro sails to the devils' island with a dog, a monkey, and a pheasant bought with rice-cakes, slays the Demon King, frees the captives, and brings home treasure for his foster-parents.
summary.zh: 老夫婦拾桃得子，桃太郎十五歲攜飯糰上路，以飯糰收犬、猿、雉為從，渡海討鬼島，斬鬼王、救俘虜、奪寶歸鄉。

sensitivity.note: Classic Japanese folktale recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: While an old woman stood by a stream washing clothes, an enormous peach came floating down the water. Poor and hungry, she remembered the little verse about distant water being bitter and near water sweet, and sang it until the fruit stopped at her feet. That evening her husband was about to cut the peach open when it burst open of its own accord and the prettiest child imaginable tumbled out with a merry laugh. 'The Gods have heard how much you desired a child,' he said, 'and have sent me to be a solace and comfort in your old age.' They called him Momotaro, Son of a Peach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'The Adventures of Momotaro' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: At fifteen the lad towered above his fellows and longed for knightly heroism. He asked leave to sail to an island in the North-Eastern Sea where devils had captured a great company of innocent people and ate many of them, meaning to kill the devils, free the captives, and bring back the plunder for his foster-parents. His father consented, sure that no devil could harm a child sent from heaven. With rice-cakes from the old woman, Momotaro won over a growling dog, then a monkey, then a pheasant - each eating half a cake and joining the expedition.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'The Triumph of Momotaro' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The pheasant flew ahead to the devils' castle and demanded surrender and broken horns, but the devils only laughed and hurled iron bars. On shore Momotaro found two daimyos' daughters weeping over blood-soaked washing, and they showed him a way into the castle. Inside, the little band fought tenaciously; many devils fell from the parapets and were dashed to pieces, and all were destroyed except the Demon King, who begged for his life and was refused. Momotaro gave the captive King into the monkey's keeping, freed the prisoners, and gathered much treasure; the dog and pheasant carried the spoils home, and his foster-parents ended their days in peace and plenty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'The Triumph of Momotaro' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Tawara Toda, My Lord Bag of Rice

region.en: Seta bridge, Lake Biwa

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: The hero Hidesato climbs over a sleeping dragon on a bridge and so wins the Dragon King of Lake Biwa's trust; with saliva-smeared arrows he slays the monstrous centipede of Mount Mikami and receives inexhaustible rice, silk, and a fireless cooking-pot.
summary.zh: 俵藤太跨過橋上臥龍不懼，龍王請其誅食其子孫之百足怪；以唾塗箭簇射腦誅之，獲寶米、寶綢、寶鍋，遂號俵藤太。

sensitivity.note: Medieval Japanese hero legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The great Hidesato came one day to the bridge over beautiful Lake Biwa and found the way blocked by a great serpent-dragon fast asleep. Without a moment's hesitation he climbed over the monster and walked on - and behind him the dragon became a man with red hair and a dragon-shaped crown, bowing with much ceremony. He was the Dragon King of Lake Biwa, who had taken a hideous shape to test for a fearless mortal; all men had fled at the sight of him, but a monstrous centipede came down from Mount Mikami, destroyed his children and grandchildren, and soon he himself would be devoured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'My Lord Bag of Rice' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the palace beneath the lake Hidesato was feasted with crystallised lotus leaves while goldfish danced and carp played the koto and samisen - until a noise like a dozen thunderclaps sent them running to the balcony: Mount Mikami was covered from top to bottom with the great coils of the centipede, fire-balls glowing in its head and its hundred feet like a chain of lanterns. Two arrows struck the monster and fell harmlessly away. Remembering the magical effect of human saliva, Hidesato put his last arrow-head in his mouth, fitted it to the bow, and took careful aim; the arrow pierced the centipede's brain, the lights in its eyes and legs went out, and the lake lay shrouded in darkness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'My Lord Bag of Rice' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a second royal feast, the Dragon King bestowed five precious gifts - two bells, a bag of rice, a roll of silk, and a cooking-pot - carried to Hidesato's home by fishes suddenly turned into men. The rice-bag was inexhaustible, the silk without end, the pot cooked without fire. Only the bells were without magic, and these were given to a temple nearby. Hidesato grew rich and famous, and people no longer called him Hidesato but Tawara Toda, My Lord Bag of Rice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. II 'My Lord Bag of Rice' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Inari, the Fox God

region.en: Inari shrines throughout Japan (symbolic pin: Fushimi Inari, Kyoto)
region.zh: 稻荷神社（象徵定位：京都伏見稻荷）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Inari, originally the God of Rice, became in the eleventh century the Fox God: foxes possess infinite vision, hear secret thoughts, and transform into beautiful women whose shadows betray them - yet the God also cures coughs, grants children, and rewards kindness with coins that turn to grass.
summary.zh: 稻荷本為稻神，十一世紀與狐神合流：狐具無限眼力、能聞人心、化為美女（唯影照水現狐形），亦能治病、送子、酬恩——賞金常化為草。

sensitivity.note: Japanese fox-superstition lore recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Inari was originally the God of Rice, but in the eleventh century he became associated with the Fox God, with attributes for good and evil, mostly for evil. All foxes possess supernatural powers to an almost limitless degree: they have the power of infinite vision, they can hear everything and understand the secret thoughts of mankind, and they possess the power of transformation and transmutation. The chief attribute of the bad fox is the power to delude human beings, and for this purpose it takes the form of a beautiful woman; if the shadow of a fox-woman falls upon water, only the fox is revealed, and if a dog sees one, the feminine form vanishes and the fox alone remains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V 'Inari, the Fox God' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yet Inari sometimes poses as a beneficent being who cures coughs and colds, brings wealth to the needy, and answers a woman's prayer for a child; he also enables little boys and girls to bear with fortitude the razor and the hot bath. He not infrequently rewards human beings for kindness to a fox - though at least one tempting coin is bound to turn quickly into grass. Demoniacal possession, kitsune-tsuki, is frequently ascribed to the evil influence of foxes: the sufferer is usually a woman of the poorer classes, and a fox is said to enter her through the breast or between the finger-nails, living a separate life and often speaking in a voice wholly different from the human.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V 'Inari, the Fox God' and 'Demoniacal Possession' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Death-Stone of Nasu Moor

region.en: Nasu moor

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: A spirit warns the priest Genno away from the Death-Stone and tells its own story: a demon fox that ruined courts in India, China, and Japan as a beautiful concubine until a Court Magician exposed her; men and beasts that touch the stone perish, until Genno's rite wins her repentance.
summary.zh: 那須高原殺生石觸之即死。行基僧玄引近石，石中妖自述：歷生於印度、支那、日本三國宮闈為惑主妖姬，終被法師識破，逐至野原化石害生。玄引誦經度化，妖悔悟發誓改過。

sensitivity.note: Japanese fox-demon legend adapted from a No drama (trans. Chamberlain), recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The Buddhist priest Genno, after much weary travel, came to the moor of Nasu and was about to rest under the shadow of a great stone when a spirit appeared: 'Rest not under this stone. This is the Death-Stone. Men, birds, and beasts have perished by merely touching it!' Genno begged for the story, and the spirit began: long ago a fair girl at the Japanese Court was called the Jewel Maiden, so wise that she understood Buddhist lore, the Confucian classics, science, and the poetry of China - and the monarch himself clasped her to his heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V 'The Death-Stone' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: At a great feast in the Summer Palace a mysterious wind blew out every lantern, and in the panic a weirdly lustrous flame darted from the Jewel Maiden's body and lit the imperial halls. From that hour the Mikado sickened, until the Court Magician declared the Jewel Maiden a harlot and a fiend who with insidious art ravaged the State and captivated the Emperor's heart. Spurned, the sorceress resumed her original shape - a fox - and ran away to the very stone on Nasu moor. 'I am the demon that once dwelt in the breast of the Jewel Maiden,' said the spirit. 'Now I inhabit the Death-Stone for evermore.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V 'The Death-Stone' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Genno gave the spirit his priestly robe and begging-bowl and conjured it to confess its former lives: in India it had been the demon to whom Prince Hazoku paid homage; in Great Cathay, Hōji, consort of the Emperor Iuwao; and at the Court of the Rising Sun, the Flawless Jewel Maiden, concubine to the Emperor Toba. She had gloated over the Mikado's coming death until the Magician's power drove her out; pursued by dogs and arrows, she sank exhausted into the Death-Stone. Genno offered flowers, burnt incense, and recited the sacred Scriptures before the stone, and the contrite spirit swore from that hour to be virtue's child alone, then vanished beneath the Stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V 'The Death-Stone' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: How Tokutaro was Deluded by Foxes

region.en: Maki moor (symbolic pin: Edo region)
region.zh: 牧野原（象徵定位：江戶近郊）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: A sceptic wagers wine and cash that foxes cannot deceive him on Maki moor; he seizes, beats, and burns a woman he believes a fox - and wakes from the ordeal on the moor, shaved bald by the foxes and the loser of his bet.
summary.zh: 德太郎不信狐之幻術，與人打賭夜赴牧野；見熟人者之女疑為狐，毆之焚之，被控殺人；一夢醒來，頭髮盡為狐剃，賭輸矣。

sensitivity.note: Japanese fox legend recorded by Mitford and retold 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Tokutaro was a complete sceptic in regard to the magical power of foxes, and his scepticism exasperated his companions into a wager: if nothing happened to him on Maki moor he was to receive five measures of wine and a thousand copper cash worth of fish; if the foxes prevailed, he would pay the same. Jeering, he accepted the bet and set out by night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V 'How Tokutaro was Deluded by Foxes' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: On reaching his destination he saw a fox run through a bamboo grove, and immediately afterwards met the daughter of the headman of Upper Horikane, who said she was going the same way. Tokutaro walked behind her vainly searching for a fox's tail, and when the girl's parents came out astonished to see their married daughter, he announced with superior wisdom that she was a fox in disguise. The parents at first refused to believe it, but he persuaded them to leave the girl in his hands while they waited in the store-closet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V 'How Tokutaro was Deluded by Foxes' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Tokutaro then seized the girl, brutally knocked her down, stamped upon her, and tortured her in every possible way, expecting every moment to see her turn into a fox; but she only wept piteously for her parents. Finding his efforts fruitless, the sceptic piled wood upon the floor and burnt her to death; her parents rushed in and bound him to a pillar, fiercely accusing him of murder. A passing priest begged the old couple to spare his life so that he might become a devout priest, and Tokutaro knelt to have his head shaved - whereupon a loud peal of laughter woke him on the open moor: the foxes had shaved him, and he had lost his bet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. V 'How Tokutaro was Deluded by Foxes' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Jizo and the Dry Bed of the River of Souls

region.en: Sai-no-Kawara, beneath the earth (symbolic pin: Shide mountain foothills)
region.zh: 賽之河原（地下，象徵定位）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Beneath the earth the souls of dead children gather pebbles and heap them into prayer-towers; every evening the oni knock the towers down, until Jizo folds the children into his shining robe and drives the red-eyed demons away with his sacred staff.
summary.zh: 地下賽之河原，夭折童魂日疊石塔為父母祈禱，每至日暮鬼怪毀塔，童子泣奔地藏；地藏以衣裹童、以錫杖驅鬼，自為冥途眾兒父母。

sensitivity.note: A Buddhist devotional legend beloved of Japanese mothers, retold 1912 by Davis with Hearn's translated hymn; category myth because it is living temple lore rather than scripture; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Jizo, the God of little children and the God who makes calm the troubled sea, is the most lovable of the Buddhist divinities. Though of Buddhist origin, he is essentially the creation of innumerable Japanese women who longed to project into the Infinite a deity who should be a divine Father and Mother to the souls of their little ones. Jizo has waived aside Nirvana and does not sit upon the Golden Lotus: through an exquisitely beautiful self-sacrifice he has become the divine playmate and protector of Japanese children, the God of smiles and long sleeves, the enemy of evil spirits, and the one being who can heal the wound of a mother who has lost her child in death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VI 'The Significance of Jizo' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Under the earth there is the Sai-no-Kawara, the Dry Bed of the River of Souls, where all children go after death. There the little ones play with the smiling Jizo and build small towers of stones, while the mothers above them pile stones around his images, for these towers represent prayers and charms against the oni. Sometimes the oni gain a momentary victory and knock down the little towers; when that happens the laughter ceases, and the children fly to Jizo for protection. He hides them in his long sleeves and, with his sacred staff, drives away the red-eyed oni.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VI 'The Dry Bed of the River of Souls' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the hymn called The Legend of the Humming of the Sai-no-Kawara, the children of two or three years and less than ten are gathered at the roots of the Mountain of Shide, crying for their parents with a voice that pierces flesh and bone. By day they heap the tower of prayers - first for father, then for mother, then for all whom they loved at home; but as the sun sinks, the demons of the hells appear and tell them their parents' mourning is the cause of their pains, then cast down the towers with clubs of iron. Then the teacher Jizo appears: 'Be not afraid, dears! I am your father and mother in the Meido, father of all children in the region of the dead' - and he folds the skirt of his shining robe about them, stretches forth his shakujo to those who cannot walk, and pets the little ones in his bosom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VI 'The Legend of the Humming of the Sai-no-Kawara' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Cave of the Children's Ghosts

region.en: The Ancient Cavern, Kyu-Kukedo-San, sea-coast cave (symbolic pin: San'in coast)
region.zh: 久金戶山古洞（海岸洞窟，象徵定位）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Far within the Ancient Cavern stands an image of Jizo with a Shinto torii and gohei before him; each night the ghosts of children creep over the sea to build towers of stones in the sand, departing before dawn because the dead fear to gaze upon the Sun Goddess.
summary.zh: 久金戶山古洞深處供地藏像，像前置鳥居與幣帛，佛道神道於此合拜。每夜童子幽靈渡海至洞中沙上疊石塔，日出前離去——死者不敢仰視天照大神之金睛。

sensitivity.note: A Japanese coastal shrine legend recorded 1912 in Davis; category myth since it is shrine lore rather than scripture; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: There is a cave in Japan known as Kyu-Kukedo-San, the Ancient Cavern, and far within its recess there is an image of Jizo with his mystic jewel and sacred staff. Before Jizo there is a little torii and a pair of gohei, symbols of the Shinto faith; but this gentle divinity has no enemies, and at the feet of the lover of children's ghosts both creeds unite in tender homage.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VI 'The Cave of the Children's Ghosts' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Here it is that the ghosts of little children meet, softly whispering as they stoop hither and thither to build their towers of stones. At night they creep over the sea from their Dry Bed of the River of Souls and cover the sand in the cavern with their ghostly footsteps, building, ever building, those prayers of stone, while Jizo smiles down upon their labour. They depart before the rising of the sun, for the dead fear to gaze upon the Sun Goddess, and most especially do these infants fear her bright gold eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VI 'The Cave of the Children's Ghosts' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Seven Gods of Good Fortune and the Treasure Ship

region.en: The Takara-bune treasure ship of New Year's Eve (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 寶船（除夕浮海，象徵定位）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Six gods and one goddess - Fukurokuju, Daikoku, Ebisu, Hotei, Bishamon, Benten, and Jurojin - ride the Treasure Ship into port on New Year's Eve laden with the hat of invisibility, the lucky raincoat, the sacred key, and the inexhaustible purse; pictures under a child's pillow bring a lucky dream.
summary.zh: 七福神（壽老人、大黑天、惠比須、布袋、毘沙門、辯才天、壽老神）乘寶船於除夕入港，載隱身笠、幸運蓑衣、神鑰、不盡袋等寶。童枕下置寶船圖可得吉夢。

sensitivity.note: A New Year festival legend-cycle recorded 1912 in Davis; category myth since these are folk deities of luck rather than scriptural beings; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The favourite theme of the Japanese artist is the Seven Gods of Good Fortune, nearly always treated with rollicking good-humour. There was Fukurokuju, with a very long head, attended by a crane, deer, or tortoise; Daikoku, who stood upon rice-bales and was accompanied by a rat; Ebisu, carrying a fish; Hotei, the merry God of Laughter, the very embodiment of 'Laugh and grow fat'; Bishamon, resplendent in armour, bearing a spear and toy pagoda; Benten, the Goddess of Beauty, Wealth, Fertility, and Offspring; and Jurojin, very similar to Fukurokuju. These seven - six Gods and one Goddess - seem to have sprung from Shintoism, Taoism, Buddhism, and Brahmanism, and apparently date from the seventeenth century.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VII 'The Gods of Good Fortune' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In connection with this theme the Japanese artist is fond of portraying the Gods of Good Fortune as jovial passengers on the Takara-bune, the Treasure Ship, which is said to come to port on New Year's Eve with no less a cargo than the Hat of Invisibility, the Lucky Raincoat, the Sacred Key, the Inexhaustible Purse, and other curious and magical treasures. At this time of year pictures of the Treasure Ship are placed under children's wooden pillows, and the practice is said to bring a lucky dream.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VII 'The Treasure Ship' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hotei, the God of Laughter and Contentment, is represented as extremely fat, carrying on his back a linen bag - ho-tei, whence his name - in which he stows the Precious Things, and sometimes merry and inquisitive children. Daikoku is shown as a prosperous gentleman with a Magic Mallet whose stroke confers wealth, standing on bales of rice with the Red Sun against his breast; and Ebisu, his son, the God of Labour, carries a fishing-rod and a great tai fish under his arm. The two are usually pictured together, god of wealth and god of honest work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XV 'Hotei' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Hidari Jingoro and the Statue that Came to Life

region.en: Jingoro's studio (symbolic pin: Kyoto)
region.zh: 左甚五郎工房（象徵定位：京都）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: The famous sculptor Hidari Jingoro carves a woman he loves and sets her own lost mirror between the chiselled robes; because the mirror had reflected her face a thousand thousand times, it had taken to itself her very body and soul, and the statue comes to life.
summary.zh: 名雕師左甚五郎暗戀路遇美女，拾其遺鏡嵌入雕像衣褶間。鏡面千萬次映照其容，竟藏其魂魄，雕成之夜石像活焉。

sensitivity.note: An artist-legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Among the legends of the miraculous in Japanese art is the story of Hidari Jingoro, the famous sculptor, whose masterpiece came to life when finished - a tale that reminds us not a little of the story of Pygmalion. Hidari Jingoro happened to fall in love with a very attractive woman whom he met in the street on his return to his studio. So fascinated was he by her rare beauty that as soon as he reached his destination he commenced to carve a statue of her, and between the chiselled robes he placed the mirror the lovely woman had dropped and which her eager lover had at once picked up. Because this mirror had reflected a thousand thousand times that fair face, it had taken to its shining surface the very body and soul of its owner, and because of these strange things the statue came to life, to the extreme happiness of sculptor and maid.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VII and ch. XIV Hidari Jingoro (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Sesshiu Paints Rats with His Tears

region.en: A Buddhist temple (symbolic pin)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Bound in a temple as a naughty boy, the future master Sesshiu uses his tears for ink and his toe for a brush; the rats he paints come alive and gnaw through the rope that holds him.
summary.zh: 雪舟少時被縛於寺中，以淚為墨、以趾為筆繪鼠；群鼠應筆而活，囓斷繩索救其出。

sensitivity.note: An artist-legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: When the great artist Sesshiu was a little boy, the story goes that he was, by way of punishment, securely bound in a Buddhist temple. Using his copious tears for ink and his toe for a brush, the little fellow sketched some rats upon the floor. Immediately they came to life and gnawed through the rope that bound their youthful creator.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VII 'The Miraculous in Japanese Art' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Dream of Rosei

region.en: The inn of Kantan (Chinese legend in Japanese No drama; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 邯鄲之宿（中國傳說・日本能劇；象徵定位）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Weary Rosei sleeps on the Magic Pillow of Dreams at the inn of Kantan and reigns fifty glorious years in a deathless country where all seasons linger - until he drinks the elixir, wakes on a common pillow, and learns that a century of bliss fades like a dream.
summary.zh: 盧生困頓宿邯鄲，枕幻夢枕而入夢：登基於長春之國，銀山金山相映，四時不謝。飲不死之藥後，一覺醒來仍卧逆旅，五十年榮華如一瞬。

sensitivity.note: A Chinese legend (Kantan/Rosei) woven into Japanese art and the No drama, adapted 1912 by Davis from Chamberlain's translation; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Rosei, in ancient times, reached the little inn of Kantan, so weary with his travel that he fell asleep as soon as his head touched the pillow. It was the Magic Pillow of Dreams, for directly Rosei was asleep an envoy approached him: the Emperor of Ibara wished to relinquish the throne and install him in his place. Rosei entered a palanquin strewn with gems of radiant hue and was borne to a wonderful country floored with golden sand and silvern pebbles, through gates inlaid with diamonds and jade, where throngs in vestments of radiant light came bearing countless gifts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VII 'The Dream of Rosei' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In that country Nature forgot her natural laws: in the east there was a silver hill over which the gold sun shone, and in the west a gold hill over which the moon shone. No spring and autumn marked the time, and over that deathless gate the sun and moon forgot their wonted speed - a land of eternal youth where no flower faded. Rosei lived and reigned for fifty years, and then a minister bade him drink of the Elixir of Life so that he might, like his subjects, live for ever. He drank amid dazzling pomp, believing he had cheated Death of his due, and gave sumptuous feasts where lovely maidens danced amid endless music and song.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VII 'The Dream of Rosei' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: But the joyous pageants were not endless after all, for eventually Rosei awoke to find himself resting upon Kantan's pillow. He that ponders well will find all life tells the self-same story: when death comes, a century of bliss fades like a dream. Rosei concluded that life is a dream and ambition a dream too, and having accepted this Buddhistic teaching, he returned to his own home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VII 'The Dream of Rosei' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Star Lovers of the Celestial River

region.en: The Celestial River (Milky Way); Tanabata festival, Japan (symbolic pin)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: The Weaving Lady Tanabata and the ox-leading Hikoboshi love too well to work; the God of the Firmament parts them along the Celestial River, letting them meet once a year on a bridge of birds - unless rain swells the flood of stars.
summary.zh: 織女與牽牛戀愛荒怠織耕，天帝怒而以天河分隔，准其每年七夕一度鵲橋相會；若雨漲天河，鵲橋不成，又需再待一年。

sensitivity.note: A Chinese-derived star myth naturalised as the Japanese Tanabata festival, recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: One of the most romantic of the old Japanese festivals is the Festival of Tanabata, the Weaving Lady, held on the seventh day of the seventh month, when freshly cut bamboos are set on the roofs or beside the houses and hung with coloured papers bearing poems in praise of Tanabata and her husband Hikoboshi. The God of the Firmament had a lovely daughter who spent her time in weaving for her august father, until one day at her loom she saw a handsome lad leading an ox and immediately fell in love with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VIII 'The Star Lovers' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her father, reading her secret thoughts, speedily consented to the marriage - but the lovers loved not wisely but too well. Tanabata neglected her weaving, and Hikoboshi's ox wandered at large over the High Plain of Heaven. The God of the Firmament became extremely angry and commanded that the too ardent lovers should henceforth be separated by the Celestial River. On the seventh night of the seventh month, provided the weather was favourable, a great company of birds formed a bridge across the river by which the lovers could meet; but if it rained, the Celestial River would become too wide even for a bridge of magpies to span, and the lovers would wait another weary year. Hence children sing at the festival: 'Tenki ni nari' - Oh, weather, be clear!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VIII 'The Star Lovers' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Robe of Feathers

region.en: Mio's pine-clad shore, Suruga

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: A fisherman steals a celestial robe hanging on a pine; without it the Moon-maiden cannot return to heaven, so he trades it for a dance - and while she sings of the thirty monarchs of the Moon Palace she rises into the sky and is gone.
summary.zh: 漁夫於三保松原松枝間拾得羽衣，不肯歸還天女。天女言著衣則忘塵俗，漁夫羞慚奉還；天女著衣起舞，歌詠月宮三十君主，舞罷乘風直上青天而杳。

sensitivity.note: The Hagoromo legend, adapted 1912 by Davis from the No drama (trans. Chamberlain); passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: It was spring-time, and along Mio's pine-clad shore there came a sound of birds. Hairukoo, a fisherman, sat down to enjoy the scene and chanced to see, hanging on a pine-tree, a beautiful robe of pure white feathers. As he was about to take it down, an extremely lovely maiden came toward him from the sea and begged him to restore the robe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VIII 'The Robe of Feathers' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fisherman refused: 'I found this robe, and I mean to keep it, for it is a marvel to be placed among the treasures of Japan.' The maiden cried pitifully that without her robe of feathers she could never return to her celestial home, but the hard-hearted fellow would not relent. At last he offered to restore it if she would dance before him, and when she asked how she could dance without her feathers, he answered suspiciously that once she had the robe she would fly away without dancing. 'The pledge of mortals may be broken,' said the maiden angrily, 'but there is no falsehood among the Heavenly Beings' - and these words put the fisherman to shame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VIII 'The Robe of Feathers' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wearing her pure white garment, the maiden struck a musical instrument and began to dance, singing of her far-away home in the Moon: of the mighty Palace of the Moon, where thirty monarchs ruled, fifteen in robes of white when the orb was full and fifteen robed in black when the Moon was waning. As she sang and played and danced she blessed Japan, that earth may still her proper increase yield. Soon her dainty feet ceased to tap upon the sand: she rose into the air, the white feathers gleaming against pine-trees and blue sky, higher and higher, until her song was hushed and she reached the glorious Palace of the Moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. VIII 'The Moon-Lady's Song' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Sentaro's Visit to the Land of Perpetual Youth

region.en: Land of Perpetual Youth beyond the sea; Jofuku's shrine, Mount Fuji (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 長生不死之國（象徵定位：富士聖護院徐福祠）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: The Chinese seeker Jofuku failed to wrest immortality from Fuji and is worshipped as a saint; Sentaro, praying at his shrine, receives a paper crane that swells to a giant bird and carries him to a land where people eat poisons and long in vain to die - he returns after three hundred years there, content with the common span of life.
summary.zh: 秦人徐福求仙藥於富士而不得，歿為當地聖者。仙太郎拜其祠得紙鶴，化巨鶴負之至無死無生之國；彼國之人食毒而不得死。仙太郎厭之歸國，已歷三百年，遂安於常壽。

sensitivity.note: A Fuji immortality legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The desire to wrest from Mount Fuji the secret of perpetual life never met with success. A Chinese, Jofuku by name, reached the sacred mountain with this object in view; he failed and never lived to return to his own country, but he is looked upon as a saint, and those bound on the same quest pray earnestly at his shrine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. IX 'Sentaro's Visit to the Land of Perpetual Youth' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sentaro on one occasion prayed at this shrine and was presented with a small paper crane, which expanded to a vast size the moment it reached his hands. On the back of this great crane Sentaro flew to the Land of Perpetual Youth, where, to his amazement, the people ate poisons and longed in vain to die. Sentaro soon grew weary of this land, returned to his own country, and resolved to be content with the ordinary span of years allotted to mankind - as well he might, considering that he had already spent three hundred years in the country where there was no death and no birth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. IX 'Sentaro's Visit to the Land of Perpetual Youth' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Visu Watches the Go Game for Three Hundred Years

region.en: Mount Fuji (symbolic pin)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Urged to 'work and pray', the woodman Visu prays only, lets his family starve, and storms off to Fuji; there he forgets everything watching two ladies play go, learns too late they were foxes, and returns to find three hundred years have buried wife and children.
summary.zh: 僧勸樵夫美寿見且作且禱；夫偏終日祈禱而荒作，妻兒飢困，遂怒而上富士。山頂見二美婦弈棋，一坐三百載；一言破局而狐遁，歸家時妻兒已葬，斧柄已化塵。

sensitivity.note: A Fuji legend recorded 1912 in Davis (Gordon Smith adaptation); the mountain-rising episode is covered by the existing record fuji-legend, so this record cuts only the three-hundred-year go-game episode; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: An old priest visited the giant woodman Visu and told him he never prayed. 'If you had a wife and a large family to keep,' said Visu, 'you would never have time to pray.' The angry priest gave him a lurid account of being reborn as a toad, a mouse, or an insect for millions of years, until Visu promised to pray; 'Work and pray,' said the priest as he took his departure. Unfortunately Visu did nothing but pray: his rice crops withered and his wife and family starved, and his wife, who had never said a harsh word before, pointed to the thin bodies of her children and bade him take up his axe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. IX 'The Adventures of Visu' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Astonished, Visu could find no reply but hot words: 'Woman, the Gods come first... I will have nothing more to do with you!' He snatched up his axe, left the hut without farewell, and climbed Fuji-yama, where a mist hid him. There, forgetting his prayers in an instant when he deemed it lucky to see a fox, he chased the creature to an open space in a wood - and found two ladies sitting by a brook playing go. Fascinated, he sat watching their long black hair and quick little hands; there was no sound but the click of pieces and the song of the running brook. After three hundred years, though to him it was but a summer's afternoon, one of the players made a false move, and he cried out, 'Wrongs, most lovely lady!' In a moment the women turned into foxes and ran away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. IX 'The Adventures of Visu' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Visu attempted to pursue them, his limbs were terribly stiff, his hair very long, his beard touching the ground, and the handle of his hardest-wood axe had crumbled into dust. He dragged himself home, but no hut was there; an old woman told him that Visu had lived three hundred years ago, gone away one day, and never come back, and that his wife and children were buried. 'The Gods have prolonged your miserable life in punishment for having neglected your wife and little children,' she hissed. Weeping, Visu said: 'I have lost my manhood. I have prayed when my dear ones starved. Old woman, remember my last words: if you pray, work too!' His white spirit is still said to haunt Fuji-yama when the moon shines brightly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. IX 'Visu's Return' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Kiyo and the Priest: the Bell of Karma

region.en: Tea-house by the Hidaka river and the temple of the Dragon's Claw hill (Kii)
region.zh: 日高川畔茶屋與龜爪山寺（紀伊）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: The tea-house beauty Kiyo wins and loses the love of a priest; tutored by a tengu of Kompira, she transforms herself into a dragon-serpent, crushes the great bell in which he hides, and melts bell and priest and herself together in her coils - the working of Karma.
summary.zh: 茶屋美妓清姬與僧相戀；僧悔而避，清姬詣不動明王、金毗羅神修咒，得化龍蛇之術。蛇軀渡河入鐘樓，壓毀鐘柱，僧匿鐘內；蛇纏鐘至紅熱，鐘熔為金汁，僧與蛇俱亡——業報之力也。

sensitivity.note: The Kiyohime legend (Dojoji type), recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Near the banks of the Hidaka, beside a hill called the Dragon's Claw, stood a far-famed tea-house whose fairest girl was Kiyo, like the fragrance of white lilies come down the mountain wind. Across the river a Buddhist temple kept a great bell six inches thick and weighing several tons; its monks were forbidden fish, meat, sake, and tea-houses. Yet one priest, returning from a shrine, saw Kiyo flitting through the tea-garden like a bright-winged butterfly; that night he could not sleep, and at last, stifling his religion, crept across the river night after night to her, finding in a woman's charms something sweeter, for the moment, than the possibility of attaining Nirvana.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. X 'A Bell and the Power of Karma' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Conscience at last stirred and vanquished passion; the priest dealt circumspectly with Kiyo to avoid her anger. All her redoubled wiles failed to rekindle his love, and she resolved on vengeance. Arrayed in a white robe she went first to a Fudo shrine, praying the fire-ringed god to show her how to kill the priest, then to the shrine of Kompira, whose long-nosed sprite, probably a tengu, taught her after many visits all the mysteries of magic and sorcery, how to change herself at will into a dragon-serpent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. X 'A Bell and the Power of Karma' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: When her exhortations only drove the priest away for the last time, Kiyo's eyes suddenly turned into the eyes of a serpent; he fled, swam the river, and hid himself inside the great temple bell. She raised her magic wand and murmured her incantation, and in a moment the sweet maiden became a dragon-serpent hissing and spitting fire, with eyes large and luminous as moons. She crawled over the garden, swam the river, and entered the belfry; her weight broke the supporting columns and the bell, with the priest inside, fell crashing to the ground. With terrible lust for vengeance she embraced the bell, her coils holding the metal as in a vice until it grew red-hot; the prayers of the captive and of his brethren availed nothing, and the bell melted and ran down into a pool of molten metal. The great power of Karma had destroyed it, and with it the priest and the dragon-serpent that was once the beautiful Kiyo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. X 'A Bell and the Power of Karma' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Yuki-Onna, the Snow-Bride

region.en: A forest village, Musashi (symbolic pin: Edo region)
region.zh: 雪國村落（象徵定位：武藏）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: In a ferryman's hut the Lady of the Snow kills the old woodworker Mosaku and spares the beautiful apprentice Minokichi on his promise of silence; years later he marries the lovely Yuki, and one lamp-lit night his memory betrays the secret - she was Yuki-Onna, and she vanishes through the smoke-hole, sparing him only for the sleeping children.
summary.zh: 船夫小屋中雪女凍斃老木匠蒔造，因其年輕貌美而饒過彥吉，惟囑守密。彥吉娶雪般美妻育十子；一夜燈下失言，妻厲聲自認即雪女，因兒女在眠而暫饒，化白霧自煙囪遁去，永不復返。

sensitivity.note: The Yuki-Onna legend recorded 1912 in Davis (after Hearn); passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Mosaku and his apprentice Minokichi journeyed to a forest some little distance from their village, and being cut off by a frozen river, took shelter in the ferryman's hut on a bitterly cold night. Mosaku fell asleep at once; Minokichi woke to a shower of snow across his face, the door blown open, and a fair woman in dazzlingly white garments standing in the room. She bent over the old man, her breath coming forth like white smoke; then she hovered over the boy, whose cry froze in his throat, for her breath was like a freezing blast. She said she had intended to treat him as she had treated the old man at his side, but forbore on account of his youth and beauty, and threatening him with instant death if he ever spoke of what he had seen, she vanished. When Minokichi touched his master's hand in the dark it was like a piece of ice: Mosaku was dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XI 'The Snow-Bride' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: During the next winter, returning home, Minokichi met a pretty girl named Yuki, going to Yedo to seek a situation as a servant. He took her to his own home and married her; she bore him ten fine children, fairer of skin than the average, and when his mother died her last words were in praise of Yuki.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XI 'The Snow-Bride' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: One night, the light of a paper lamp on her face, Minokichi recalled the strange experience of the ferryman's hut: 'Yuki, you remind me so much of a beautiful white woman I saw when I was eighteen. She killed my master with her ice-cold breath. I am sure she was some strange spirit, and yet to-night she seems to resemble you!' Yuki flung down her sewing. A horrible smile on her face, she bent close and shrieked: 'It was I, Yuki-Onna, who came to you then, and silently killed your master! Oh, faithless wretch, you have broken your promise, and if it were not for our sleeping children I would kill you now! Remember, if they have aught to complain of at your hands, on a night when the snow falls I will kill you!' Then she changed into a white mist and, shrieking and shuddering, passed through the smoke-hole, never to return.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XI 'The Snow-Bride' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Willow Wife

region.en: A village under a great willow (symbolic pin)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Heitaro saves his beloved willow from the bridge-builders and is rewarded with a wife who will not answer questions about her origin; when the ex-Emperor Toba demands the tree for a Kwannon temple in Kyoto, the villagers fell it, and Higo dies with the ax-strokes, leaving Heitaro a daughter and an unanswerable love.
summary.zh: 平太郎力保村中古柳不遭斧斤，夜得柳女為妻，育女千代。後攝政為建觀音堂徵巨木，村人斬柳；柳女於房中與樹同痛，唯言吾愛不可斬，香消而逝。

sensitivity.note: The Willow Wife legend recorded 1912 in Davis (Gordon Smith adaptation); passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In a certain Japanese village there grew a great willow-tree, loved by the people for many generations as a summer meeting-place and a winter umbrella of sparkling snow. Heitaro, a young farmer who lived near, had entered into a deep communion with the imposing willow, burning joss-sticks beneath its branches and kneeling in prayer. When the villagers wanted the tree for a bridge, he hid his face in his hands - 'My dear willow-tree for a bridge, one to bear the incessant patter of feet? Never!' - and offered his own trees instead, and the willow was spared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIII 'Willow Wife' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: One night under the great willow a beautiful woman appeared beside him, shy and wanting to speak, and told him his heart had always been there. Night after night they met until he asked her to be his wife; 'Call me Higo (Willow) and ask no questions, for love of me,' she said, 'I have no father or mother, and some day you will understand.' They were married and blessed with a child, Chiyodo, and were the happiest people in all Japan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIII 'Willow Wife' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then great news came: the ex-Emperor Toba wished to build a temple to Kwannon in Kyoto, and the villagers resolved to contribute their great willow. No argument could save it, and that night Higo woke her husband with a piercing cry: 'The room is full of whispers. They are cutting down the willow-tree. Look how its shadow trembles in the moonlight. I am the soul of the willow-tree! The villagers are killing me. Dear Heitaro, the pain, the pain! Put your hands here, and here. Surely the blows cannot fall now?' Sobbing 'My Willow Wife!' he held her while she said, 'Such a love as ours cannot be cut down, however fierce the blows. I shall wait for you and Chiyodo - my hair is falling through the sky! My body is breaking!' There was a loud crash outside; the willow lay green and dishevelled upon the ground, and Willow Wife had gone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIII 'Willow Wife' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pine-Tree Lovers of Takasago

region.en: Takasago, Harima coast

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: At Takasago a fisherman's daughter mats a dress of pine-needles for her wedding day; the swimmer Teoyo, chasing a heron, is washed ashore beneath the pine and weds her; the pair rake a needle-couch together into extreme old age, and after death their souls return each full moon to whisper and rake beside the tree.
summary.zh: 高砂漁家女松江以松針織嫁衣；遊女千代慕松江，游泳渡海昏厥，浪送至松下得救，遂結連理。夫婦偕老，每夜攜小耙松下鋪臥具；歿後每逢月圓，雙魂攜耙歸來，絮語如昔。

sensitivity.note: The Takasago pine legend behind the No drama, recorded 1912 in Davis (Gordon Smith adaptation); passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In ancient days there lived at Takasago a fisherman, his wife, and little daughter Matsue. Nothing pleased Matsue more than to sit under the great pine-tree, gathering the never-tiring pine-needles, out of which she fashioned a beautiful dress and sash: 'I will not wear these pine-clothes until my wedding-day.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIII 'The Pine-tree Lovers' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Teoyo, a youth who dearly loved adventure, stood on the steep shore of Sumiyoshi watching the flight of a heron and thought it would be delightful to swim across the sea and discover the land over which it had flown. He dived in and swam until the waves spun and the sky bent down to touch him, and he lay unconscious on the water - but the waves were kind, and pressed him on and on until he was washed up at the very place where Matsue sat under the pine-tree. She dragged him beneath the sheltering branches and set him on a couch of pine-needles, and when he had recovered, he did not go back: after some happy months he married Matsue, who wore her dress and sash of pine-needles on the wedding morn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIII 'The Pine-tree Lovers' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The older they grew the more they loved each other. Every night when the moon shone they went hand in hand to the pine-tree and, with their little rakes, made a couch for the morrow. One night the great silver face of the moon peered through the branches and looked in vain for the old lovers; their rakes lay side by side, but the Pine-Tree Lovers did not come - they had gone home to an everlasting resting-place on the River of Souls. They had loved so well and so splendidly, in old age as in youth, that the Gods allowed their souls to come back again and wander round the pine-tree that had listened to their love for so many years. When the moon is full they whisper and laugh and sing and draw the pine-needles together, while the sea sings softly upon the shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIII 'The Pine-tree Lovers' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Soul of the Mirror

region.en: A Kyoto lodging-house with a haunted well

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: In a drought-filled Kyoto house the Shinto priest Matsumura's well never runs dry - and never runs dry because a Poison Dragon enslaves the soul of an old mirror to lure the thirsty to their death; freed when the dragon is exiled, the soul Yayoi asks that the mirror be polished and given to the Shogun Yoshimasa, and warns the priest to flee before the storm sweeps his house away.
summary.zh: 京都大旱，神主松村宅井獨不涸——井中毒龍脅迫鏡靈誘人斃命。龍既逐，鏡靈彌生請淨其鏡獻將軍義政；臨別囑速遷，明日宅果為洪水所沒。

sensitivity.note: A mirror legend recorded 1912 in Davis (Gordon Smith adaptation); passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: The shrine of Ogawachi-Myojin fell into decay, and the Shinto priest in charge, Matsumura, journeyed to Kyoto to appeal to the Shogun for a grant for restoration. His family lodged in a house said to be unlucky: many tenants had thrown themselves into the well on the north-east side. In the great drought of that summer the well remained full to overflowing while river-beds and other wells failed, and poor people begged water there without diminishing it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIV 'The Soul of a Mirror' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day a dead body was found in the well - a servant come to fetch water. When Matsumura inspected the well, the water stirred with a strange rocking movement, and in the clear surface he saw reflected the form of a fair young woman touching her lips with beni. Her strange smile made him feel dizzy and almost irresistible was the desire to fling himself into the water to reach and hold her. He struggled free, had the well fenced round, and forbade all drawing. When rain at last came, a woman knocked at his door in the storm: she had never desired to lure anyone to death, she said - the Poison Dragon in the well had forced her against her will, and now the Gods had compelled the dragon to live elsewhere. Search would find her body in the well, and her reward would follow his care for it. The well-cleaners found some ancient hair ornaments and an old metal mirror; on the back Matsumura made out the characters 'third month, the third day' - Yayoi, the Month of Increase, and the woman had called herself Yayoi: the Soul of the Mirror.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIV 'The Soul of a Mirror' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: He had the mirror resilvered and polished and laid in a box in a particular room, and Yayoi appeared before him more beautiful than ever. She was the soul of a mirror once owned by Lady Kamo of the Imperial Court and become an heirloom of the Fujiwara House until, in the conflict of the Hogen period, she was thrown into the well and forgotten, all the horrors of the Poison Dragon's tyranny piled upon her. She begged that the mirror be presented to the Shogun Yoshimasa, a descendant of her former possessors, and warned Matsumura to leave his home at once, for it was about to be washed away by a great storm. He left; his dwelling was swept away; and when he presented the mirror with its written history, the Shogun was so pleased that he gave the priest rich presents and money enough to rebuild his temple.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIV 'The Soul of a Mirror' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mirror of Matsuyama

region.en: A remote village in Japan (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 松山（日本偏鄉，象徵定位）

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: A father brings home Japan's first mirror; the dying mother tells her daughter to look into it whenever she is lonely and she will see her - the grieving girl does so, is accused by a jealous stepmother of witchcraft, and is exonerated when she shows the mirror to her father.
summary.zh: 父自京帶回鏡一面；母臨終囑女曰：思我則照鏡，即可見母。繼母妒之，誣其行巫術咒己；父查問，女出鏡示父，言每照則見母親溫顏，心乃安。誤會冰釋，一家和睦。

sensitivity.note: A mirror legend recorded 1912 in Davis; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: In ancient days there lived in a remote part of Japan a man and his wife, blessed with a little girl who was the pet and idol of her parents. Called away on business to distant Kyoto, the father promised his daughter that if she were good and dutiful to her mother he would bring her back a present she would prize very highly. He returned with a wonderful doll, a lacquer box of cakes, and - a wonder of wonders - a metal mirror whose convex surface shone brightly, with pine-trees and storks on its back. The good man's wife, who had never seen a mirror before, thought another woman looked out upon her until her husband explained the mystery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIV 'The Mirror of Matsuyama' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Not long after, the woman became very ill, and just before she died she called her little daughter: 'Dear child, when I am dead take every care of your father. You will miss me when I have left you. But take this mirror, and when you feel most lonely look into it and you will always see me.' In due time the man married again, and his wife was not kind to the stepdaughter; but the little one would retire to a corner and eagerly look into the mirror, where it seemed to her she saw her dear mother's face, not drawn in pain as on the death-bed, but young and beautiful.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIV 'The Mirror of Matsuyama' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The stepmother, chancing to see the child crouching over the shining thing and murmuring to herself, fancied she was performing magical art - perhaps making an image and sticking pins into it - and told her husband his wicked child was trying to kill her by witchcraft. Surprised in her room, the girl slipped the mirror into her sleeve, and for the first time her doting father grew angry. Then she told him the truth: 'The mirror you gave my mother, and which she on her death-bed gave to me. Every time I look into its shining surface I see the face of my dear mother, young and beautiful. When my heart aches, mother's face, with its sweet, kind smile, brings me peace.' The man understood and loved his child the more; even the stepmother was ashamed and asked forgiveness, and trouble for ever departed from the home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XIV 'The Mirror of Matsuyama' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Chujo Hime, the Incarnation of Kwannon

region.en: Temple of Taima-dera, Yamato

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: Cruelly treated by her stepmother, the nun Chujo Hime retired to Taima-dera and worked the lotus-thread embroidery of the Buddhist Paradise, a design so exquisite that the Gods themselves are believed to have helped her hand - for she was, according to legend, an incarnation of Kwannon.
summary.zh: 中之宮姫受繼母虐待，出家當麻寺，繡蓮絲極樂淨土曼荼羅，精妙絕倫，世謂神明相助——蓋以其為觀音化身也。

sensitivity.note: A temple hagiographic legend recorded 1912 in Davis; category myth since it is temple lore rather than scripture; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Chujo Hime, a Buddhist nun, is generally regarded as the greatest early Japanese artist of embroidery, and, according to legend, she was an incarnation of Kwannon. She met with much cruel treatment from her stepmother until she finally retired to the temple of Taima-dera, and there worked upon the wonderful lotus thread embroidery depicting the Buddhist Paradise. The design is so exquisite that we can easily understand the Japanese belief that the Gods helped this great artist in her work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XV 'An Incarnation of Kwannon' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Benten and the Dragon of Enoshima

region.en: The island of Enoshima, risen from the sea

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: A dragon in a sea-cave devours the children of Koshigoe; in the sixth century Benten causes an earthquake, descends from the clouds, marries the dragon, and ends the slaughter - and from the sea rises the island of Enoshima, sacred to the Goddess of the Sea ever since.
summary.zh: 腰越村有龍居洞中，吞食童子。六世紀辯才天降大地震，乘雲而下，入洞與龍成婚，以善念化之，食童遂止。海中湧出江之島，自此為海神聖地。

sensitivity.note: A shrine-legend of Enoshima recorded 1912 in Davis; category myth since it is shrine lore rather than scripture; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Benten, the Goddess of the Sea, is also one of the Seven Divinities of Luck, romantically referred to as the Goddess of Love, Beauty, and Eloquence. She is represented riding on a dragon or serpent, which may account for the fact that in certain localities snakes are regarded as sacred; images depict her with eight arms, six hands holding bow, arrow, wheel, sword, key, and sacred jewel, and two hands reverently crossed in prayer. Her shrines are usually to be found on islands.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XV 'Benten' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: In a certain cave there lived a formidable dragon which devoured the children of the village of Koshigoe. In the sixth century Benten was determined to put a stop to this monster's unseemly behaviour: having caused a great earthquake, she hovered in the clouds over the cave, then descended, entered the cavern, married the dragon, and was thus able, through her good influence, to put an end to the slaughter of little children. With the coming of Benten there arose from the sea the famous Island of Enoshima, which has remained to this day sacred to the Goddess of the Sea.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XV 'Benten and the Dragon' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Festival of the Dead

region.en: The Bon festival, houses, cemeteries and rivers of Japan (symbolic pin)

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: At death the soul must cross the River of Three Roads, paying Old Woman Sodzu-Baba or losing its pilgrim's garments; the Festival of the Dead (July 13-15) welcomes the ghosts home with tiny meals, feeds the friendless dead of Gakido - as Mokenren's mother was freed when he fed the priests - and sends them away at midnight in little boats with lanterns at the prow.
summary.zh: 人死魂渡三途川，付六文錢於奪衣婆；不然白衣被奪掛樹。七月十三至十五日盂蘭盆，備小膳迎歸魂，施食於無主餓鬼——目連救母即其源。十五夜以載膳小舟送靈，燈浮川海。

sensitivity.note: The Bon festival complex recorded 1912 in Davis; category myth since the Sodzu-Baba and Mokenren elements are folk-Buddhist narrative rather than canonical scripture; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: At death the body is washed, shaven, and arrayed in the garment of a pilgrim, with a wallet containing three or six rin hung round the neck and buried with the deceased; for all who die, children alone excepted, must journey to the Sanzu-no-Kawa, the River of the Three Roads. On its dismal bank Sodzu-Baba, the Old Woman of the Three Roads, awaits the coming of souls together with her husband, Ten Datsu-Ba; if the three rin are not paid, she takes away the white garments of the dead and, regardless of entreaties, hangs them on trees. Add Emma-O, the Lord of the Dead, and the terrors of the Buddhist hells, and it is no surprise that the gentle Japanese founded a festival to afford a pleasant, if all too brief, respite from the horrors of Hades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVII 'The Festival of the Dead' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The festival takes place from July 13 to 15. New mats of rice straw are spread on the altars and household shrines, and every home is provided with a quaint, minute meal in readiness for the great company of ghosts; lanterns are lit, incense burned, and water poured in the cemeteries. On the evening of the 15th the ghosts of the Circle of Penance, Gakido, are fed, and those who have no friends among the living. There is a legend for this: Dai-Mokenren, a great disciple of Buddha, was permitted to see the soul of his mother in the Gakido, but every time she tried to eat the food he gave her it turned to fire and ashes; told to feed the ghosts of the great priests of all countries on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he did so, and found his mother dancing for joy. In this happy dance after tribulation we trace the origin of the Bon-odori, which takes place on the third night of the festival.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVII 'The Festival of the Dead' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the evening of the third day preparations are made for the departure of the ghosts. Thousands of little boats are packed with food and loving messages of farewell; into these boats step the departing ghosts, and loving hands set the frail craft upon river, lake, or sea - a small lantern glowing at the prow, pale blue clouds of incense floating from the stern. Down all the creeks and rivers the phantom fleets go glimmering to the sea; all the sea sparkles to the horizon with the lights of the dead, and the sea wind is fragrant with incense.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVII 'The Festival of the Dead' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: The Peony Lantern

region.en: Yanaka-no-Sasaki and the cemetery of Shin-Banzui-In, Edo
region.zh: 江戶谷中與坂尺・新番所作

source.work: F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: The samurai Shinzaburo, kept from visiting Tsuyu by a jealous old doctor, learns of her death too late; at the Festival of the Dead she and her maid Yone come each night behind a peony lantern, his servant spies a half-corpse in the mosquito-net, and when the servant sells back the sacred charms the dead woman's bones twine about his neck - love between the living and the dead ends in the destruction of the living.
summary.zh: 萩原新三郎與常陸女戀，為老醫所阻，女憂鬱而歿。盆節之夜，牡丹燈籠引女與侍女音來會；僕窺蚊帳見半身枯骨。後僕貪百兩，毀佛印，女骨纏郎頸而同寢。

sensitivity.note: The Botan Dorō ghost story, Japanese in local colour though inspired by a Chinese tale, retold 1912 by Davis after Hearn; passages are condensed paraphrases of a public-domain retelling, presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Tsuyu, Morning Dew, was the only daughter of Iijima. When her father married again she found she could not live happily with her stepmother, and a separate house was built for her, where she lived with her servant-maid Yone. One day the family physician Yamamoto Shijo brought a handsome young samurai, Hagiwara Shinzaburo, and the young people fell in love at sight; at parting Tsuyu whispered, 'Remember! if you do not come to see me again I shall certainly die!' Etiquette would not allow Shinzaburo to visit alone, and the old doctor, having seen more than the young people supposed, purposely refrained from keeping his promise. Believing her lover unfaithful, Tsuyu slowly pined away and died, and Yone soon followed her mistress; they were buried side by side in the cemetery of Shin-Banzui-In.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVIII 'Morning-Dew' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the first day of the Festival of the Dead Shinzaburo set food on the Shelf of Souls and hung out lanterns, and waited in the warm moonlit night. Suddenly the stillness was broken by kara-kon, kara-kon, the soft patter of women's geta: over the hedge he saw two women, one carrying a long lantern with silk peonies stuck in at the upper end. It was Tsuyu and Yone - each, as it turned out, told by the same old doctor that the other was dead. They entered the house and remained that night, returning home a little before sunrise; night after night they came, always Yone carrying the shining peony-lantern, always departing at the same hour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVIII 'The Dead Return' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: One night Tomozo, a servant living next door, peeped through a crack in the sliding door: within the mosquito-net his master talked with a woman whose face was that of one long dead, her fingers a bunch of jangling bones, and only her upper body of substance, below the waist a dim moving shadow.
