A second figure sprang up and made for Tomozo's eye at the chink, and he fled shrieking to Hakuodo Yusai, a man well versed in all manner of mysteries, who told him that his master was a doomed man if the woman proved a ghost, for love between the living and the dead ends in the destruction of the living. Shinzaburo sought the quarter where the women said they lived and found only the two tombs of Shin-Banzui-In, one adorned with the very peony-lantern - their 'very small house' in Yanaka-no-Sasaki was a grave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVIII 'The Mystery is Revealed' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The high-priest Ryoseki gave Shinzaburo a small gold image of Buddha to wear next his skin, the Treasure-Raining Sutra to recite every night, and a bundle of sacred texts to paste over every opening in the house. That night the ghostly geta pattered at the doors in vain - the sacred words held them back, and he heard Yone tell her mistress that his love had changed. Then Yone went night after night to Tomozo and threatened him till his wife counselled him to bargain: for a hundred ryo the wicked servant took the gold Buddha, took down one of the sacred texts, and buried the sutra. With their entry began again the horrible love of the dead, presided over by the power of Karma; next morning Tomozo found his master dead under the mosquito-net, beside him the white bones of a woman, and the bones of Morning Dew twined round the neck of one who had loved her too well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XVIII 'The Betrayal' (Davis 1912); not verbatim.

title.en: Urashima Taro and the Dragon Palace

summary.en: The fisher-lad Urashima of Midzunoe spares a tortoise, is carried to the Dragon Palace as reward, and marries the princess Otohime in a land where all four seasons linger at once. Three days there are three hundred years on earth; opening his wife's forbidden jewel-box releases his old age, and he dies on the shore of a world he can no longer recognise.

sensitivity.note: Ancient Japanese folktale with official-annals variants (Nihongi Book X); passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations (Davis 1912; Aston 1896), presented for comparative mythology.

passages.text: Urashima, a fisher-lad of the little village of Midzunoe in Tango province, caught a tortoise in his nets; because tortoises live many thousands of years, he spared the creature and let it return to the sea. As he dozed at his oars a sweet voice called his name: the tortoise, able to speak, thanked him for his kindness and offered to carry him to the ryūgū, the Palace of the Dragon King. Riding the tortoise's back he glided through the sea at tremendous speed, and his clothes never once grew wet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the Sea King's palace the red bream, flounder, sole and cuttlefish came out to welcome him, and the Dragon King led him to an inner chamber where the princess Otohime sat in garments of red and gold, the colours of a wave under sunlight. She explained that the tortoise had been herself, testing his kindness of heart, and as reward for his virtue she offered to be his bride in a land of eternal youth. Fishes in ceremonial robes bore coral trays of delicacies, music was played, and the wedding cup of sake was drunk on the white sand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The marvel of that country was that all four seasons lingered together: eastward plum and cherry bloomed with butterflies above the blossom; southward the trees stood in full summer and the cricket sang; westward the maples burned like fire; northward lay snow and a pond of ice. After three days Urashima remembered his old parents and asked leave to go home. Otohime wept and begged him to stay one day more, but he promised to return, and she gave him a keepsake, the Tamate-bako, the Box of the Jewel Hand, forbidding him ever to open it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Mounting the tortoise he reached his own country, but his father's cottage had vanished and only the little stream remained. A passer-by told him that a fisher-lad named Urashima had gone to sea three hundred years ago and was drowned, and all his kin lay long in their graves; then he remembered that in the divine land one day was a hundred years. Hearing the murmur of the sea, he thought Otohime called him, and that if he opened the box it might reveal the way back. He untied the red silk thread and lifted the lid: a little white cloud rushed out and rolled away over the sea, and the sacred promise broken, the handsome youth became old and wrinkled, staggered toward the waves, and fell dead upon the shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan, ch. XXVII (1912); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
Urashima Taro is Japan's classic otherworld-voyage tale, and one of its oldest: traces of the story appear in the official annals (Nihongi, Book X, where a fisher named Urashima-no-ko visits the Eternal Land of Tokoyo and returns aged) and in two famous Man'yōshū laments that take the story for granted, so that the ballad must be centuries older than its oldest written forms. In the popular version the fisher-lad of Midzunoe in Tango province spares a tortoise; the tortoise is the sea-princess Otohime in disguise, come to test his kindness, and she repays him with a voyage to the Dragon Palace of the sea-god, her father.

The Dragon Palace (ryūgū) is an otherworld of perfect abundance and suspended time: fish in ceremonial robes serve the wedding feast, and the seasons stand together in one landscape — spring in the east, summer in the south, autumn in the west, winter in the north — a ritual image of the world renewed and unchanging, akin to the Evergreen Land of Tokoyo in the annals. Urashima marries Otohime and dwells in this bliss for what he believes are days.

The return home supplies the tale's tragic engine. Three days in the palace are three hundred years on earth; the village, the parents, the whole world he knew have passed away. Otohime's parting gift, the Tamate-bako (jewel-box), is a taboo-object: it holds either his vanished years or the road back to the sea — the tellings differ — and it must never be opened. Lonely among strangers and hearing the sea call like a wife's voice, Urashima opens it. A white cloud escapes, and his mortality, banked for three centuries, settles on him at once; in the Davis retelling he falls dead on the shore; in the Man'yōshū he becomes a crane and departs, and his wife flies up from the sea as a tortoise; in the Nihongi he simply grows old and dies, a witness of Tokoyo's time-slip.

The tale functions as Japan's great meditation on time and death: bliss bought by kindness, forfeited by curiosity, and unrecoverable because the otherworld's clock cannot be reconciled with ours. It also aetiologises the summer sea-longsing: the shore of Midzunoe, the boy's tomb and casket were still shown at a Kanagawa temple in Chamberlain's day, and Mount Fuji's name 'never-dying' echoes the same immortality-longing in the Taketori tale. As a comparative text it sits with the Celtic otherworld voyages (Oisín in Tír na nÓg is nearly the same plot) and with the boxed-years motif found from Polynesia to China, making it one of the strongest cross-tradition matches in the Japanese corpus.

functions: Etiology of the time-slip: explains human mortality and the irreversibility of age through a contrast between divine and human time (one palace day = one hundred years).
Charter for kindness-to-animals motifs in Japanese folk ethics: the test of the tortoise rewards compassion with otherworld hospitality.
Ritual image of world-renewal: the four seasons abiding together in the Dragon Palace mirror Tokoyo, the Evergreen Land of the annals, as an image of unchanging abundance.
Festival and shore-lore anchor: Urashima's tomb, fishing-line and casket were shown at a Kanagawa temple, and the tale is recited in summer sea-songs and Noh (Urashima, Takasago's companion pieces).
